intro: Belgrade's protected trees read like a short course in the city's overlapping histories: a two-century oak that predates the square built around it, a princely plane tree that outgrew the legend crediting the prince himself, and two yews planted a century later, flanking a cathedral gate as an accidental match of male and female. Across the river in Zemun, once Habsburg territory rather than Serbian, a single 1991 designation protects nine unrelated evergreens as one grouping. None of the four costs anything to see, and none was planted with a visitor in mind.
meta_description: Belgrade's most remarkable trees: a 200-year-old oak, a prince's plane tree with 17 iron supports, cathedral yews, and Zemun's protected evergreens.
question_answer: Belgrade's oldest protected tree is the pedunculate oak on Cvetni trg in Vračar, over 200 years old and first protected as a natural monument in 1980, the last living remnant of the oak and ash forest that covered this part of the city before 19th-century development cleared it. It predates every building and street around it.
question_meta: A 200-year-old oak on a Belgrade square, the last living trace of the forest the city was built over, holds the oldest documented tree title.
question_context: The pedunculate oak on Cvetni trg holds its claim on documentation rather than drama. Belgrade's park authority has protected it continuously since 1980, reconfirmed in a 2001 review, on the strength of a genuinely old and genuinely singular fact: the oak and ash woodland that once covered much of the Vračar district was cleared for streets and a marketplace in the early 19th century, and this is the one tree from that vanished forest still standing. Every other candidate for Belgrade's oldest tree trails it by a documented margin. The plane tree at Topčider, often cited as the city's most impressive, is younger by several decades even under its most generous dating, and its planting date is itself disputed by up to 36 years depending on the source. The two yews at Belgrade Cathedral and the protected grouping in Zemun's park are all closer to a century old than two. So while none of Belgrade's four protected trees has a precisely documented planting year, the Cvetni trg oak's two-century estimate, and its unmatched position as the sole survivor of an entire vanished ecosystem, put it clearly ahead of the rest.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Belgrade?
faq.a: The pedunculate oak on Cvetni trg in Vračar, over 200 years old and protected as a natural monument since 1980, the last living remnant of the oak and ash forest cleared from this part of the city in the early 19th century.

faq.q: Why do two yews flank Belgrade Cathedral's entrance?
faq.a: They were planted as a pair around the turn of the 20th century and happen to be one male and one female tree, protected as natural monuments since 1979.

faq.q: What holds up the plane tree at Topčider?
faq.a: Seventeen iron posts, installed in 1881, still support its 49 metre crown, since a tree that size cannot carry that spread on its own indefinitely.

faq.q: Are Belgrade's protected trees free to visit?
faq.a: Yes, all four stand in public parks, a public square, or a church courtyard, with no entry charge.

trees.name: The Oak of Cvetni Trg

location.address: Cvetni trg, Njegoševa ulica, Vračar, Belgrade

trees.story: Belgrade's oldest protected natural monument stands on a market square, not in a forest or a palace garden. The pedunculate oak on Cvetni trg, in the Vračar district, is what is left of the oak and ash woodland that once covered this whole part of the city before Belgrade's 19th-century expansion cleared it for streets and a marketplace; virtually everything else that grew alongside it is gone, and this one tree carries the entire ecosystem's memory alone. It stands about 25 metres tall with a trunk 4 metres around, first protected in 1980 and reconfirmed in a 2001 review, its branches now held with steel cables against the ordinary damage of two centuries. Vračar itself grew up around the tree rather than the other way round: the oak was already old when the square took shape, and the streets, the market stalls and the apartment blocks all arranged themselves at a respectful distance from a trunk that outdates every building currently standing near it. It gets no palace, no royal legend, no famous name attached, just a metal fence, a protection order first signed in 1980, and roughly two centuries of continuous growth on a spot that could easily have gone under concrete instead.
trees.transport: Vračar district, Njegoševa ulica; about a 15 minute walk from Slavija Square

photo.attribution: BuhaM, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Great Plane of Topčider

location.address: In front of Milošev Konak, Topčiderski park, Savski venac, Belgrade

trees.story: Seventeen iron posts have held up the crown of Belgrade's largest tree since 1881, propping branches that would otherwise have snapped under their own 49 metre spread a century and a half ago. The plane tree stands in front of Milošev Konak in Topčider, the hunting lodge Prince Miloš Obrenović built as Serbia was clawing its way toward autonomy from the Ottoman Empire, and a popular story credits the prince himself with planting it from a single weak seedling in an old lime kiln. The dates do not cooperate: Miloš left Topčider for exile in 1839, and the tree itself, dated to 1834 by the same municipal records that later declared it a natural monument, was most likely planted after he had already gone. What survives the legend is the tree itself, a trunk 7.35 metres around, a height of 34 metres, and a canopy that shades nearly 1,900 square metres of the park, nearly two centuries into a life that has outlasted a princedom, a kingdom, and two versions of Yugoslavia. Declared a natural monument in 1979, it remains, by most measures, the biggest single tree in the Serbian capital.
trees.transport: Topčider district, Savski venac; about a 20 minute drive or bus ride from central Belgrade

photo.attribution: Andy Mabbett (Pigsonthewing), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Two Yews of Belgrade Cathedral

location.address: Courtyard entrance, Saborna crkva (Belgrade Cathedral), Kneza Sime Markovića, Belgrade

trees.story: Two yews flank the gate into Belgrade Cathedral's courtyard, one on each side of the entrance on Kneza Sime Markovića street, and between them they demonstrate something most visitors never think to check: yews come in two sexes, and these are one of each. The slightly taller tree, at 13.3 metres, is male; the shorter one, 11.8 metres, is female, and unlike most paired ornamental plantings nobody chose them to match on purpose, they were simply planted together around the turn of the 20th century and grew into their roles. Both were formally protected as natural monuments in 1979, valued specifically for being unusually large, healthy specimens of a species rarely found this size inside a dense city center rather than out in a forest or a rural churchyard. The Cathedral itself, built between 1837 and 1840, is one of Belgrade's most visited churches, and its courtyard sees a steady stream of visitors who walk directly between the two trees without necessarily noticing that the one on their left and the one on their right are, in the plainest botanical sense, a couple.
trees.access: Free, public church courtyard, viewable during normal visiting hours
trees.transport: Stari Grad, Kneza Sime Markovića; a 5 minute walk from Knez Mihailova street

photo.attribution: BrankaVV, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.name: The Yews of Zemun Park
trees.story: Zemun's Gradski park protects nine trees as a single natural monument, not one, an unusual designation that covers five European yews and four groups of Caucasian wingnut scattered through a park most Belgraders think of simply as Zemun's green center. All are roughly 110 years old, planted around the turn of the 20th century when Zemun was still an Austro-Hungarian town across the river from the Kingdom of Serbia rather than the Belgrade municipality it later became. Caucasian wingnut, a fast growing riverside tree from the Caucasus and northern Iran, is rare enough in Serbian parks that finding four separate stands of it in one place justified protecting the whole grouping in 1991 rather than picking out a single champion specimen. The yews do the more familiar work, dark, dense evergreen shapes among the park's roughly 1,300 other trees, old enough and large enough to count as genuine heritage rather than ordinary planting. Nothing here has a named legend attached, no prince, no botanist, no famous visitor, just a formal designation covering an entire pocket of a park that has quietly outlasted the empire it was planted under.
trees.transport: Zemun, on the Danube waterfront; about a 25 minute bus ride from central Belgrade

photo.attribution: Milica Buha (BuhaM), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
